title: How Taiwan Can Win the Strait
gist: Holmes Liao and Dennis Blair argue Taiwan's plan to build large 7,000-ton warships and 3,000-ton frigates is strategically wrong -- large ships have become 'sitting ducks' against modern ISR/missile threats -- and that Taiwan should instead mass-produce 700-1,000-ton stealthy corvettes (each under $200 million versus $2 billion for a large warship) modeled on Finland/Sweden's fleets, citing the Falklands, Operation Praying Mantis, the Moskva sinking, and Ukraine's Black Sea campaign as evidence that smaller, dispersed naval forces can deny a stronger adversary control of contested waters.

themes.theme: Large ships are increasingly obsolete in restricted waters

insights.claim: Liao and Blair argue that advances in ISR, electronic warfare, drones, and missiles are making large surface ships easier to detect, track, and attack, turning Taiwan's traditional destroyer/frigate fleet into a strategic liability in the narrow, roughly 100-mile-wide Taiwan Strait.
insights.speaker: Holmes Liao
insights.so_what: Core investment/procurement thesis: large-hull naval shipbuilders face a structural threat from ISR/missile proliferation in any contested littoral scenario, not just Taiwan -- relevant to global naval shipbuilding capital allocation.
insights.quote: Yet large surface ships are vulnerable in the narrow waters of the Taiwan Strait—a problem compounded by advances in technology that are making them easier to detect, track, and attack.

insights.claim: Taiwan's current shipbuilding plans include a new 7,000-ton warship and as many as 12 3,000-ton light frigates, which the authors say are impediments to the radical transformation the Chinese threat requires.
insights.speaker: Holmes Liao
insights.so_what: Names specific programs (7,000-ton warship, 12 light frigates) that the authors argue should be curtailed -- a concrete policy target for Taiwan defense-budget watchers and shipbuilders bidding on these contracts.
insights.quote: The Taiwanese navy is planning to invest heavily in large surface combatants, including a new 7,000-ton warship and as many as 12 3,000-ton light frigates.

insights.claim: The U.S. Navy's Constellation-class frigate program illustrates the cost trap of building survivable large ships: budgeted at roughly $1 billion per ship, costs rose to about $1.5 billion each before the program was canceled, and even at that price the ships lacked the capability to fight an advanced adversary in restricted waters.
insights.speaker: Holmes Liao
insights.so_what: A directly comparable, dated cost-overrun/cancellation case study ($1B to $1.5B per ship, then canceled) that investors in naval shipbuilders should weigh when assessing large-combatant program risk broadly, not just for Taiwan.
insights.quote: The U.S. Navy's Constellation-class frigate program, for example, budgeted roughly $1 billion per ship; the cost eventually rose to about $1.5 billion each before the Constellation program was canceled.

insights.claim: Taiwan's entire annual shipbuilding budget is projected at $1.5 billion -- roughly equal to the cost of a single U.S. Constellation-class frigate -- underscoring the resource mismatch of pursuing large-hull programs.
insights.speaker: Holmes Liao
insights.so_what: A stark budget-scale comparison ($1.5B/year total vs. $1.5B for one comparable large ship) that quantifies why Taiwan cannot realistically pursue a large-combatant-centric fleet at meaningful scale.
insights.quote: In comparison, the spending on Taiwan's entire shipbuilding program is projected to be $1.5 billion annually.

themes.theme: The proposed alternative: distributed stealthy corvettes

insights.claim: The authors recommend Taiwan build stealthy corvettes weighing 700 to 1,000 tons, armed with missiles and drones, combined with shore-based mobile launchers, antiship-missile-armed aircraft, and eight submarines, to create a dispersed, hard-to-destroy defense system for sea denial.
insights.speaker: Holmes Liao
insights.so_what: A specific, actionable force-design alternative (700-1,000 ton corvette fleet + land-based missiles + submarines) that could reshape Taiwan defense procurement priorities and the addressable market for smaller-combatant and missile-system suppliers.
insights.quote: Taipei should build stealthy corvettes weighing between 700 and 1,000 tons, armed with missiles and drones, that are harder to detect and target but can retain enough firepower to attack Chinese ships crossing the strait.

insights.claim: Taiwan has already commissioned eight missile patrol corvettes with an innovative catamaran hull design (faster and more stable), each delivered to the navy for less than $200 million, versus an estimated $2 billion for a single 7,000-ton warship -- a roughly 10x cost difference per hull.
insights.speaker: Holmes Liao
insights.so_what: A hard cost-comparison data point (<$200M vs $2B per hull) that makes the economic case for the corvette strategy extremely concrete and quotable for defense-budget debates.
insights.quote: Each of these ships has been delivered to the navy for less than $200 million, whereas a single 7,000-ton warship will cost an estimated $2 billion.

insights.claim: Four more of Taiwan's catamaran-hull corvettes are scheduled to be commissioned by the end of 2026, and the authors argue that sustained production would drive down unit costs further while allowing incorporation of new weapons and sensors in each successive batch.
insights.speaker: Holmes Liao
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete near-term delivery milestone (4 more corvettes by end of 2026) that can be used to track whether Taiwan is actually executing the recommended strategy.
insights.quote: Four more of these vessels are scheduled to be commissioned by the end of the year. Taiwan's shipbuilding industry can rapidly produce these vessels, and the more it builds, the more efficient it will become.

insights.claim: Finland and Sweden are cited as successful models of corvette-centric navies that have deterred and harassed a much larger adversary (Russia), including escorting away Russian ships that entered their waters and lodging diplomatic protests, backed by extensive surveillance and decision-support networks.
insights.speaker: Holmes Liao
insights.so_what: Provides a working real-world template (Nordic corvette navies) that Taiwan -- and by extension any smaller power facing a larger adversary -- could emulate; relevant precedent for evaluating similar small-navy defense strategies elsewhere.
insights.quote: With navies built around corvette-class-sized ships, Finland and Sweden have successfully stood up to Russian pressure, harassing Russian submarines that have violated their territorial seas.

themes.theme: Historical evidence: small/dispersed forces vs. large ships

insights.claim: In the 1982 Falklands War, after a British submarine sank Argentina's cruiser General Belgrano, Argentina kept the rest of its surface fleet -- including the carrier Veinticinco de Mayo -- close to coastal waters or in port for the remainder of the war, showing how a single strike can politically constrain an entire fleet.
insights.speaker: Holmes Liao
insights.so_what: A historical mechanism (single high-value-ship loss causing fleet-wide risk aversion) directly transferable to how Taiwan or any navy might react psychologically/politically to losing a large warship in the Strait.
insights.quote: After a British submarine sank the Belgrano, Argentina decided to keep much of the rest of its surface fleet, including the carrier, closer to coastal waters or in ports for the rest of the war.

insights.claim: In 1988's Operation Praying Mantis, the U.S. Navy combined surveillance, aircraft, ships, and precision weapons to sink or badly damage several Iranian surface vessels including two large frigates in a single day, demonstrating the lethality of an effective 'kill chain' against large ships.
insights.speaker: Holmes Liao
insights.so_what: Illustrates the destructive power of a modern kill chain (sensors + comms + precision weapons) against large ships -- directly analogous to the ISR/missile capability China is building against Taiwan's fleet.
insights.quote: In a single day, U.S. forces sank or badly damaged several Iranian surface vessels operating in the confined waters of the Gulf, including two large frigates.
insights.locator: Sitting Ducks section, Praying Mantis example

insights.claim: In 2006, a Hezbollah cruise missile struck the Israeli corvette Hanit off Lebanon, killing four sailors, but the crew contained the damage and the ship survived; Israel's response was not to abandon corvettes but to build larger, better-armed ones.
insights.speaker: Holmes Liao
insights.so_what: Shows that losing/damaging a smaller ship carries far less political and strategic cost than losing a large one, and that navies historically respond to such attacks by iterating on the small-ship class rather than abandoning it.
insights.quote: The attack did not lead Israel to abandon corvettes; instead, it built larger, better-armed corvettes.

insights.claim: Ukraine's Black Sea campaign after Russia's 2022 invasion -- combining land-based antiship cruise missiles, uncrewed surface vessel swarms, aerial drones, and external intelligence -- pushed much of Russia's fleet farther from Ukraine's shores and sank the flagship Moskva, proving a weaker power can achieve sea denial without a comparable fleet.
insights.speaker: Holmes Liao
insights.so_what: The single most directly relevant precedent for Taiwan's strategy: a weaker naval power achieved effective sea denial against a much stronger navy using dispersed, asymmetric, largely uncrewed systems -- the central evidentiary pillar of the authors' argument.
insights.quote: Ukraine's Black Sea campaign after Russia's invasion in 2022 showed that a weaker power can constrain a stronger one in contested waters without commanding the sea or possessing a comparable fleet.

insights.claim: In the ongoing Iran conflict, despite the U.S. and Israel severely damaging Iran's surface navy early on, Iran has retained the ability to threaten shipping and disrupt access to the Strait of Hormuz using dispersed missiles, drones, patrol craft, and mine-laying boats.
insights.speaker: Holmes Liao
insights.so_what: Another live example reinforcing the thesis that dispersed asymmetric naval assets retain disruptive capability even after a stronger power destroys the conventional surface fleet -- relevant to ongoing Strait of Hormuz shipping/energy risk.
insights.quote: The United States and Israel severely damaged Iran's surface navy early in the conflict, but they have had difficulty eliminating dispersed missiles, drones, patrol craft and mine-laying boats.

themes.theme: Institutional and political barriers to reform

insights.claim: The authors argue the obstacles to transforming Taiwan's navy are more institutional than technical: large ships are politically attractive because they bring shipyard contracts, ribbon-cutting ceremonies, and visible proof of government commitment, whereas drones and mobile missile launchers are publicly invisible.
insights.speaker: Holmes Liao
insights.so_what: Identifies a political-economy bias (visibility bias) toward large-ship procurement that could persist regardless of strategic logic -- a structural headwind for the corvette-centric reform the authors advocate, and a pattern likely generalizable to other countries' defense procurement.
insights.quote: Because they are highly visible, large ships are attractive to politicians. They bring contracts for shipyards, ribbon-cutting ceremonies, a sense of national achievement.

insights.claim: Taiwan's proposed 2027 defense budget is likely to surpass 3 percent of GDP, and the legislature passed a $25 billion special defense budget in May 2026 -- a significant sum, though down from the $40 billion originally proposed by the executive branch.
insights.speaker: Holmes Liao
insights.so_what: Concrete, dated fiscal figures (3%+ of GDP, $25B special budget vs $40B proposed) for tracking Taiwan's actual defense-spending trajectory and legislative appetite relative to executive branch ambitions.
insights.quote: Taiwan's proposed 2027 defense budget is likely to surpass three percent of GDP, and the legislature also passed a $25 billion special defense budget in May.

insights.claim: Taiwan's first domestically built submarines are currently behind schedule, which the authors argue is an inevitable but non-disqualifying challenge for complex-vessel programs that should not derail continued investment.
insights.speaker: Holmes Liao
insights.so_what: Flags execution risk (schedule slippage) in Taiwan's indigenous submarine program -- relevant for tracking program timelines and supplier/contractor performance.
insights.quote: Production of Taiwan's first domestically built submarines, for instance, is currently behind schedule.
